label: Institution
name: Brazilian Catholic Apostolic Church
summary:
The Brazilian Catholic Apostolic Church (Portuguese: Igreja Católica Apostólica Brasileira, ICAB), founded in 1945 by ex-Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Duarte Costa — is Brazil's largest independent Catholic church, representing a permanent schism from the Roman Catholic Church that established an alternative Catholic institution maintaining sacraments, apostolic succession, and liturgy while rejecting papal authority and adopting Brazilian nationalist and social reform orientations.

Carlos Duarte Costa was a Brazilian bishop who became increasingly critical of the Roman Catholic Church's alignment with Brazil's Conservative elites and its silence on social justice issues in the 1930s-1940s. He was excommunicated by Pope Pius XII in 1945 and subsequently founded the ICAB as an independent Catholic church that would prioritize Brazilian national identity, clerical marriage, vernacular worship (before Vatican II), and social justice — several positions that the Vatican II Council eventually adopted for Roman Catholicism.

The ICAB has grown into a substantial Brazilian institution, claiming hundreds of thousands of members and ordaining both men and women as priests. Its founder's progressive theological positions — vernacular Mass, married clergy, social justice orientation — were remarkably prescient of subsequent Roman Catholic reforms, though the schism was never healed. Brazil's complex Catholic landscape — the world's largest Catholic country (approximately 125 million Catholics) but one where Pentecostalism has grown dramatically — makes the ICAB an interesting case study in Catholic institutional alternatives.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Brazilian Catholic Apostolic Church — founded in 1945, anticipating Vatican II reforms in vernacular Mass and social justice orientation, growing into Brazil's largest independent Catholic institution — is historically significant as a monument to Catholic reform movements and independent Catholicism in Latin America.
